pos: adj. and n. (destitute, in want; rendering Hebrew ebyon, dal)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon nyd, necessity, compulsion. The Hebrew ebyon means one who asks — the needy man is defined by his dependence, not by a statistic.
biblical_def: Needy is one of the covenant's most protected categories. The law does not pretend the poor will vanish; it commands generosity precisely because they will not: “the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee… Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy” (Deu 15:11). Oppressing a needy hired servant is forbidden outright (Deu 24:14). And the LORD does not merely legislate on their behalf; He rises: “For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD” (Psa 12:5). The sigh of a man too weak to bring suit is itself a summons in the court of heaven. Most striking is how the psalmists claim the word for themselves — David, king of Israel, writes “I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me” (Psa 40:17). Neediness before God is not a class a believer escapes; it is the permanent posture of every soul that prays.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines needy as distressed by want of the means of living, very poor, indigent — and notes the duty of relieving the needy as a plain requirement of the divine law.
webster_full: NEED´Y, a. Distressed by want of the means of living; very poor; indigent; necessitous.
Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor and to thy needy. Deut. xv.
2. Requisite; necessary. Obsolete in this sense.
scriptures: For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.
Psa 12:5
For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him.
But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.
Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, whether he be of thy brethren, or of thy strangers that are in thy land within thy gates:
corruption_summary: Need converted into a policy abstraction on one side and a personality flaw on the other — so that the hand Deuteronomy commands to open wide is replaced by an agency, or closed altogether in the name of self-sufficiency.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 15:11 addresses a hand, not a system. Thou shalt open thine hand wide. Where care of the needy is wholly delegated to institutions, the command has not been fulfilled at scale; it has been outsourced, and the giver loses precisely the sanctification the command was designed to work in him. The opposite corruption is more recent: a therapeutic register that treats needy as a defect of character, a label for people who ask too much. Scripture's needy man is not diagnosed. He is defended.

The recovery runs through Psalm 40:17, where a king calls himself poor and needy. Neediness is the truth about every creature, and the believer who has learned it will neither despise the poor nor be ashamed to be counted among them. Psalm 12:5 supplies the motive that no policy can: the sighing of the needy moves God to arise. Whoever oppresses them is contending with a Litigant who has already announced His verdict.
roots_summary: Hebrew ebyon (H34), one who asks or longs, the destitute; dal (H1800), thin, weak, low — the two standing words for the covenant poor.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebyon (H34) — needy, destitute; from a root meaning to be willing or to long, so the needy man is one reduced to asking (Deu 15:11).
Hebrew dal (H1800) — low, weak, thin; the poor man of Leviticus, who must not be favoured in judgment either (Lev 19:15).
Hebrew ani (H6041) — afflicted, humble; often paired with ebyon as the psalmists' self-description (Psa 40:17).
usage: “Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother” — a hand is commanded, not a system.
“For the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD” — a sigh is a summons in heaven's court.
“I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me” — a king's permanent posture.

pos: adj. (feeling the want of food; rendering Hebrew ra'eb, Greek peinao)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hungrig. Scripture uses bodily hunger as its steadiest picture of the soul's condition — a want that cannot be argued away and must be fed.
biblical_def: Hungry in Scripture is both a literal emergency and the Bible's chief figure for spiritual desire. God's care for the literally hungry is stated without qualification: “he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness” (Psa 107:9). Job's friends indict a man precisely for withholding bread from the hungry (Job 22:7), which shows how the covenant measured righteousness. Then Mary's song turns the word into an announcement of the great reversal: “He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away” (Luk 1:53) — the kingdom feeds whoever comes empty-handed and sends away whoever comes full. The Lord Jesus makes that the fourth beatitude: “Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled” (Mat 5:6). Note what is not blessed — the possession of righteousness, but the hunger for it. And God's sovereign self-sufficiency stands behind it all: “If I were hungry, I would not tell thee” (Psa 50:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hungry as having a keen appetite for food, and figuratively as having an eager desire — noting that lean or barren land is called hungry.
webster_full: HUN´GRY, a. Having a keen appetite; feeling pain or uneasiness from want of food.
2. Having an eager desire.
3. Lean; emaciated, as if reduced by hunger.
4. Not rich or fertile; poor; barren; requiring substances to make it produce; as a hungry soil.
scriptures: Mat 5:6
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
Luk 1:53
He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.
For he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness.
Job 22:7
Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry.
corruption_summary: Spiritual hunger anesthetized by abundance — a church so well-fed on entertainment and information that it no longer feels the want the fourth beatitude requires.
corruption_paragraphs: Mary's song contains a warning that prosperous Christians read too quickly: the rich He has sent empty away. Not punished — sent away empty, because they arrived full. The great obstacle to being filled has never been unworthiness; it is satiety. A man surrounded by content, opinion, and constant stimulation may lose the capacity to feel hunger at all, and the fourth beatitude blesses only the hungry. Fullness of the wrong kind is the most efficient way to remain unfed.

The literal claim of the word must not be spiritualized away either. Job 22:7 treats withholding bread from the hungry as a chargeable offence, and Psalm 107:9 makes feeding them a divine action the church is meant to imitate. Both senses converge in the Lord Jesus, who fed multitudes bread and then told them plainly that He Himself was the bread — refusing to let His hearers keep the miracle and miss the Giver.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'eb (H7457), hungry, famished; Greek peinao (G3983), to hunger, to crave — the beatitude's verb, a present participle of continuous appetite.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'eb (H7457) — hungry, famished; used of the soul as well as the body (Psa 107:9).
Greek peinao (G3983) — to hunger, be needy, crave; in Mat 5:6 a continuous present, a hunger that keeps returning.
Greek chortazo (G5526) — to fill, satisfy, originally to feed with fodder; the promise attached to the hunger, they shall be filled.
usage: “Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness” — the hunger is blessed, not the possession.
“He hath filled the hungry… and the rich he hath sent empty away” — satiety is the obstacle.
“Thou hast withholden bread from the hungry” — a chargeable offence in the covenant.

pos: adj. (weak, without strength; rendering Hebrew kashal, rapheh, Greek asthenes)
etymology: From Latin flebilis, lamentable, from flere, to weep. The English word carries a sob in its root — feebleness is weakness that grieves.
biblical_def: Feeble describes strength that has failed, and Scripture watches with great care what men do with the feeble among them. Amalek's crime was precisely this: “he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee… and he feared not God” (Deu 25:18) — attacking the stragglers, which the text treats as the definitive mark of godlessness. Israel at her best does the opposite, carrying the feeble captives on asses to Jericho (2Ch 28:15). Sanballat sneers, “What do these feeble Jews?” (Neh 4:2), and the wall goes up anyway. Job's great commendation, before his own collapse, was that his words had “strengthened the feeble knees” (Job 4:4) — a phrase Isaiah and Hebrews both take up as a command to the church. And Proverbs quietly commends the conies, “but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” (Pro 30:26): feebleness that knows where to hide is wiser than strength that does not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines feeble as weak, destitute of much physical strength, and extends it to whatever is faint, imperfect, or wanting in force — a feeble light, a feeble voice, a feeble effort.
webster_full: FEE´BLE, a. Weak; destitute of much physical strength.
2. Infirm; sickly; debilitated by disease.
3. Debilitated by age or decline of life.
4. Not full or loud; as a feeble voice. 5. Wanting force or vigor; as a feeble effort.
scriptures: How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.
Job 4:4
Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees.
Neh 4:2

And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?
The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks;
corruption_summary: Strength made the measure of worth, so that the feeble are counted a burden — the Amalekite calculation, which Scripture names as the settled proof that a man feareth not God.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 25:18 gives the plainest test of a civilization in the Bible: what does it do to the ones at the back? Amalek did not fight Israel's soldiers; he struck the feeble behind, and the text supplies the diagnosis in five words — and he feared not God. Any calculus that measures a life by its productive strength arrives eventually at the same place, however clinical its vocabulary, and Scripture has already filed it under the fear of God or its absence.

The church's calling is stated in Job's commendation and repeated as command: strengthen the feeble knees. That is pastoral work, not sentiment — words that uphold him that was falling. And Nehemiah 4:2 is a permanent encouragement to congregations that know their own weakness. Sanballat's assessment was not wrong; they were feeble Jews. The wall was finished in fifty-two days regardless, because feebleness is no obstacle to God, only to the men who despise it.
roots_summary: Hebrew rapheh (H7504), slack, hanging down — the feeble hands and knees of Isa 35:3; kashal (H3782), to stumble; Greek asthenes (G772), without strength.
roots_lines: Hebrew rapheh (H7504) — slack, drooping; the feeble knees of Job 4:4, taken up in Isa 35:3 and Heb 12:12 as a command to the church.
Hebrew kashal (H3782) — to totter, stumble, be feeble; the stragglers Amalek struck (Deu 25:18).
Greek asthenes (G772) — without strength; Paul's word for the weak brother and for Christ's power made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
usage: “Even all that were feeble behind thee… and he feared not God” — the test of a civilization.
“Thou hast strengthened the feeble knees” — Job's commendation, and the church's command.
“What do these feeble Jews?” — an accurate assessment; the wall went up anyway.

pos: n. and v. (deficiency, lack; to be destitute of; rendering Hebrew chaser, machsor)
etymology: From Old Norse vant, lacking. The Authorized Version uses want in its older and stronger sense — not desire, but deficiency — and the difference governs the most quoted verse in the Psalter.
biblical_def: Want in the Authorized Version means lack, not wish, and Psalm 23:1 turns on it: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” — not I shall get whatever I desire, but I shall lack nothing the Shepherd judges necessary. Read as modern English it becomes a promise of indulgence; read as the translators meant it, it is a promise of sufficiency, which is far better and far harder. Psalm 34:10 supplies the same doctrine with a memorable contrast: “The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing” — the strongest hunters go short while the seekers are supplied, and the qualifier any good thing is God's definition of good, not ours. The word also carries covenant curse: Deuteronomy threatens service to enemies “in want of all things” (Deu 28:48). And Job, at his most desolate, names the want of a shelter (Job 24:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines want first as deficiency — the absence of that which is necessary or useful — and only afterward as desire or wish, marking the older sense as primary.
webster_full: WANT, n. Deficiency; defect; the absence of that which is necessary or useful.
2. Need; necessity; the effect of deficiency.
3. Poverty; penury; indigence.
4. The state of not having. 5. That which is not possessed, but is desired or necessary.
scriptures: Psa 23:1
A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing.

Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the LORD shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee.
Job 24:8
They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter.
corruption_summary: The semantic drift of one English word turning Psalm 23 into a promise of appetite satisfied — the exegetical root of the prosperity gospel, read straight out of a mistranslation the reader makes for himself.
corruption_paragraphs: This is a rare case where a corruption enters not by bad theology but by ordinary language change. In 1611 want meant lack; in modern English it means desire. A reader who supplies today's sense to Psalm 23:1 hears a guarantee that he will never be denied what he wants, and from there the prosperity gospel is only a short step — a divine Shepherd contracted to supply appetites. The Hebrew forecloses it: lo echsar, I shall not lack. Sufficiency, not indulgence.

The corrected reading is far more comforting, because it holds in a hospital and a famine. The sheep does not lack anything the Shepherd knows it needs, which is compatible with lying down in a valley of the shadow of death, and Psalm 34:10 attaches the same qualifier — any good thing, as God reckons good. Deuteronomy 28:48 shows the true opposite of the promise: not unfulfilled desire, but a people serving their enemies in want of all things.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaser (H2637), to lack, be without — the verb of Psa 23:1; machsor (H4270), need, poverty; Greek hustereo (G5302), to come short.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaser (H2637) — to lack, decrease, be without; lo echsar, I shall not lack (Psa 23:1), the same verb as the manna that left no lack (Exo 16:18).
Hebrew machsor (H4270) — need, want, poverty; what Proverbs promises the slack hand and the hasty man alike.
Greek hustereo (G5302) — to fall short, be destitute; Paul's I have learned… both to abound and to suffer need (Php 4:12).
usage: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” — I shall not lack; the promise is sufficiency.
“The young lions do lack… but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing” — and He defines good.
“In hunger, and in thirst… and in want of all things” — the covenant curse.

pos: n. and v. (want, deficiency; to be destitute of; rendering Hebrew chaser, Greek leipo)
etymology: From Middle Dutch lak, deficiency, blemish. In Scripture the word is used of manna, of knowledge, of wisdom, and of the one thing a rich young man was missing.
biblical_def: Lack is deficiency, and Scripture applies it in four directions worth noticing. First, to the manna, where God's provision produced a supernatural equity: “he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack” (Exo 16:18) — a verse Paul later applies to Christian giving. Second, to knowledge, in one of the most severe sentences the prophets utter: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (Hos 4:6), where the fault is laid not on the ignorant but on the priests who rejected knowledge and withheld it. Third, to wisdom, with a standing remedy attached: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” (Jas 1:5) — God neither rations the gift nor scolds the asker. Fourth, to the soul's one deficiency, in the rich young ruler's question: “what lack I yet?” (Mat 19:20). He kept the commandments and still lacked; the answer was not another duty but a Person to follow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lack as want, destitution, need, failure — and as a verb, to be destitute of, to want, to need.
webster_full: LACK, n. Want; destitution; need; failure; as a lack of bread.
LACK, v.t. To want; to be destitute of; not to have or possess.
2. To blame; to find fault with. Obsolete.
LACK, v.i. To be in want. The young lions do lack and suffer hunger.
scriptures: And when they did mete it with an omer, he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack; they gathered every man according to his eating.
Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
Jas 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
The young man saith unto him, All these things have I kept from my youth up: what lack I yet?
corruption_summary: A generation taught that it lacks nothing essential — and a religious culture that has quietly redefined the lack Hosea names, treating ignorance of Scripture as a style of piety rather than a cause of destruction.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 4:6 is regularly quoted as though the fault lay with the uninformed. Read the whole verse: because thou hast rejected knowledge… seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God. The indictment falls on the priests. A ministry that keeps the people entertained and doctrinally hungry is not merely underperforming; the prophet says the people are destroyed. That is the standing judgment on preaching that never teaches, and no amount of goodwill relieves it.

Matthew 19:20 exposes the subtler lack. The young man had kept the commandments from his youth and knew something was still missing — what lack I yet? His deficiency was not moral effort but allegiance, and the answer cost him everything he had built. James 1:5 then puts the remedy for every lack within reach of the weakest saint: ask, of a God who gives liberally and does not upbraid. The believer's lacks are real; none of them is unaddressed.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaser (H2637), to lack, decrease; Greek leipo (G3007), to leave behind, be wanting — James' word for lacking wisdom; hustereo (G5302), to come short.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaser (H2637) — to lack, be without; the manna miracle of Exo 16:18, where gathering much and little came to the same.
Greek leipo (G3007) — to leave, be destitute of; if any of you lack wisdom (Jas 1:5), and that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing (Jas 1:4).
Greek hustereo (G5302) — to fall short; the rich young ruler's what lack I yet? (Mat 19:20).
usage: “He that gathered little had no lack” — the manna's supernatural equity.
“My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” — and the priests are the ones indicted.
“What lack I yet?” — the answer was not a duty but a Person.

pos: n. (disease, ill health; rendering Hebrew choli, machalah, Greek astheneia, nosos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon seoc, ill. Scripture treats sickness as a real intruder from the fall, under God's hand, and never as a mere mechanism.
biblical_def: Sickness in Scripture is neither meaningless nor simply punitive. It stands under God's government: He promises to take sickness from the midst of an obedient Israel (Exo 23:25; Deu 7:15) and threatens it in the covenant curses (Deu 28:61). But the canon carefully forbids the flat inference that sickness proves personal sin. Elisha, the prophet of God, “was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died” (2Ki 13:14) — a faithful man, a fatal illness, no rebuke attached. Asa's case supplies the actual warning, and it is not about medicine: “in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” (2Ch 16:12). The fault was the order, not the doctors. The gospel then reveals where sickness is finally dealt with: “Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses” (Mat 8:17). And James gives the church its ordinary practice — call for the elders, and let them pray (Jas 5:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sickness as disease, illness, or a morbid state of the body, and notes its figurative use for a disordered state of anything — the sickness of a nation or of the heart.
webster_full: SICK´NESS, n. Disease; illness; the state of being diseased; the state of the body in which its functions are disturbed or deranged.
2. A particular disease; as a fatal sickness.
3. Nausea; a disposition to vomit.
4. A disordered state; as the sickness of the heart.
scriptures: Mat 8:17
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.
And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.

Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face, and said, O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.
Jas 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
corruption_summary: Two errors from one root — the faith-healing teaching that makes sickness a proof of unbelief, and the secular reading that empties it of any meaning at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity and faith-healing movements teach that healing is guaranteed in the atonement for this life, so that continuing sickness convicts the sufferer of insufficient faith. It is a cruel doctrine and the text refutes it: Elisha died of his sickness; Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick; Timothy was told to take a little wine for his often infirmities; and Paul's own thorn was not removed but answered with sufficient grace. Matthew 8:17 is true and its full harvest is eschatological — the tomb is empty and the graves are not yet.

The opposite error strips sickness of meaning entirely, leaving only biology and management. Scripture will not have that either. Asa is the case in point, and the point is frequently mistaken: he is not condemned for consulting physicians but for seeking them and not the LORD. Means are legitimate; means without prayer are Asa's error. James 5:14 shows the ordinary Christian practice that holds both together — the elders, prayer, and oil, in the name of the Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew choli (H2483), sickness, from chalah, to be weak — the word of Isaiah 53's Man of sorrows; Greek astheneia (G769), want of strength; nosos (G3554), disease.
roots_lines: Hebrew choli (H2483) — sickness, grief; in Isa 53:3 the Servant is acquainted with grief, literally with sickness.
Hebrew machalah (H4245) — disease, infirmity; the sickness the LORD promises to take from Israel's midst (Exo 23:25).
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity, sickness; Matthew applies it to Christ bearing our infirmities (Mat 8:17).
usage: “Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses” — true, and its full harvest is not yet.
“In his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” — the fault was the order.
“Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders” — the church's ordinary practice.

pos: n. (a disorder of the body; rendering Hebrew machalah, madveh, Greek nosos)
etymology: From Old French desaise, literally dis-ease, the loss of ease. The word is a picture before it is a diagnosis: the body no longer at rest in itself.
biblical_def: Disease in the Authorized Version is chiefly bound to Egypt and to the Exodus. God attaches a covenant name to Himself at the very moment He speaks of it: “I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exo 15:26) — Jehovah-Rapha, and the title is given in the context of disease withheld, not merely disease cured. Deuteronomy sets both sides of the covenant in the same terms: the LORD will take away all sickness from the obedient (Deu 7:15) and bring the diseases of Egypt upon the rebellious (Deu 28:60). Chronicles supplies the two royal case studies. Asa was “diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD” (2Ch 16:12); Jehoram was told he would have great sickness by disease of his bowels (2Ch 21:15). In every case the disease is real, physical, and under a personal government.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disease first by its literal composition — the want of ease, uneasiness, distress — and then as a morbid state of the body in which the organs do not perform their natural functions.
webster_full: DISEASE´, n. In its primary sense, pain, uneasiness, distress, and so used by Spenser; but in this sense obsolete.
2. The cause of pain or uneasiness; distemper, malady, sickness, disorder; any state of a living body in which the natural functions of the organs are interrupted or disturbed.
3. A disordered state of the mind or intellect, by which the reason is impaired.
4. In society, vice; corrupt state of morals.
scriptures: And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.
Moreover he will bring upon thee all the diseases of Egypt, which thou wast afraid of; and they shall cleave unto thee.
And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.
And thou shalt have great sickness by disease of thy bowels, until thy bowels fall out by reason of the sickness day by day.
corruption_summary: The disease model extended from the body to the soul, so that sin is reclassified as pathology — something a man has rather than something he does — and repentance is replaced by treatment.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is entirely willing to speak of the heart as sick and of sin's effects in medical figures; Isaiah 1 describes the nation as wounded from head to foot. But the figure never dissolves responsibility. The modern move is different in kind: it reclassifies drunkenness, rage, and lust as diseases proper, which relocates them from the will to the constitution and substitutes management for repentance. Where that translation is complete, the gospel has nothing to offer, because the diseased need a physician but only sinners need a Saviour — and the Lord Jesus used both words on purpose in the same sentence.

The recovery is not a denial of bodily illness or of genuine affliction of mind, both of which Scripture treats with great tenderness. It is the refusal to let the category swallow the moral one. Exodus 15:26 holds the balance exactly: real diseases, really withheld or sent, by a personal LORD who names Himself the Healer. Asa's failure is the standing caution — his disease was genuine and exceeding great, and his sin was that he sought the physicians and not the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew machalah (H4245), disease, sickness; madveh (H4064), the diseases of Egypt; Greek nosos (G3554), disease — healed by Christ in the Gospels as a sign of the kingdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew machalah (H4245) — disease, infirmity; the covenant blessing removes it (Deu 7:15) and the curse restores it (Deu 28:60).
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal; the divine title Jehovah-Rapha is given precisely in the context of disease (Exo 15:26).
Greek nosos (G3554) — disease; the Lord healed all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people (Mat 4:23).
usage: “I am the LORD that healeth thee” — the title is given where disease is withheld.
“In his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” — means without prayer.
“All the diseases of Egypt, which thou wast afraid of” — the covenant curse named.

pos: n. (soundness of body; and in Scripture, deliverance and welfare; rendering Hebrew yeshuah, marpe, arukah)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon haelth, from hal, whole — the same root as whole, hale, and holy. Health is wholeness, and Scripture uses it far beyond the body.
biblical_def: Health in the Authorized Version is often salvation. The psalmist's refrain calls God “the health of my countenance” (Psa 42:11; Psa 43:5) — the Hebrew is yeshuah, salvation, the root of the name Jesus — and asks that God's “saving health” be known among all nations (Psa 67:2). The English word, rooted in whole, is exactly right for this: what God gives is wholeness, and bodily soundness is only its outermost layer. Proverbs then applies health to wisdom and to speech: the LORD's words are “health to all their flesh” (Pro 4:22), the fear of the LORD is “health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones” (Pro 3:8), and — most searching — “the tongue of the wise is health” (Pro 12:18), set against words that pierce like a sword. Speech in Scripture is a medical instrument. It heals or it wounds, and there is no neutral setting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines health as that state of an animal body in which the parts are sound and duly perform their functions — and adds the Scriptural senses of spiritual soundness, salvation, and divine favor.
webster_full: HEALTH, n. That state of an animal or living body, in which the parts are sound, well organized and disposed, and in which they all perform freely their natural functions.
2. Sound state of the mind; natural vigor of faculties.
3. Sound state of the mind in a moral sense; purity; goodness.
4. Salvation or divine favor, or grace which cheers God's people. Psalm xliii.
scriptures: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
Psa 67:2
That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
Pro 4:22
For they are life unto those that find them, and health to all their flesh.
corruption_summary: Health enthroned as the highest good and stretched to cover every disapproval — whatever is disliked becomes unhealthy — while the saving health of Psalm 67, wholeness in God, drops out of the word entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: Two drifts have hollowed the word. First, bodily health has become for many the organizing devotion of life, pursued with a discipline and hope that Scripture reserves for God — and it is a devotion certain to be disappointed, since every body fails. Second, the therapeutic register has borrowed the vocabulary of medicine for moral judgments it does not wish to state as moral: relationships and behaviours are called healthy or unhealthy where Scripture would say righteous or sinful. The substitution feels kinder and is in fact weaker, because a diagnosis calls for management while a sin calls for repentance and can be forgiven. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic vocabulary in order to rebut it -->

The recovery is in the etymology and in the Psalter together. Health is wholeness, and wholeness is a Person's gift — the health of my countenance, and my God. That reading lets a dying saint be in perfect health in the sense that matters most, and it lets Proverbs 12:18 stand as the practical corollary: since the tongue of the wise is health, ordinary Christian speech is either medicine or a sword, and never nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew yeshuah (H3444), salvation, deliverance — rendered health in the Psalms; marpe (H4832), a cure, healing; arukah (H724), the new flesh that closes a wound.
roots_lines: Hebrew yeshuah (H3444) — salvation, deliverance; the health of my countenance (Psa 42:11) and thy saving health among all nations (Psa 67:2).
Hebrew marpe (H4832) — a cure, remedy, health; the tongue of the wise (Pro 12:18) and a sound heart as the life of the flesh (Pro 14:30).
Hebrew arukah (H724) — healing, restoration, literally the new flesh growing over a wound; the prophets' word for national recovery (Jer 30:17).
usage: “The health of my countenance, and my God” — health is a Person before it is a condition.
“Thy saving health among all nations” — the missionary petition of Psalm 67.
“The tongue of the wise is health” — speech is medicine or a sword, never nothing.

etymology: From Latin calamitas, damage, disaster — anciently connected with calamus, a stalk, and the ruin of a standing crop. Scripture's calamity likewise falls on what was standing.
biblical_def: Calamity is sudden ruin, and Scripture insists on two things about it. First, it is timed: “their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand” (Deu 32:35) — a verse whose weight the Reformed tradition has long felt, since the wicked stand only until an appointed moment. Proverbs repeats the suddenness for the man who despises reproof: “shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy” (Pro 6:15). Second, calamity is the hour that reveals both God and neighbours. David's testimony is the pattern for the believer: “They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the LORD was my stay” (Psa 18:18). Proverbs adds a startlingly practical word about friendship — in the day of calamity a near neighbour is better than a far brother (Pro 27:10). And Wisdom's own laughter at the calamity of those who refused her (Pro 1:26) is among the most sobering sentences in the canon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calamity as any great misfortune or cause of misery — distinguishing it as generally denoting a more lasting and extensive evil than misfortune, and often applied to public evils.
webster_full: CALAM´ITY, n. Any great misfortune, or cause of misery; generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evils, as loss of crops, earthquakes, conflagrations, defeat of armies, and the like.
2. Misfortune; distress; adversity.
The word calamity usually denotes a more lasting evil than misfortune.
scriptures: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the LORD was my stay.
Pro 6:15
Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy.
Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.
corruption_summary: Disaster read as either meaningless accident or as a simple verdict on its victims — both readings refuse the harder biblical answer, that calamity is governed, timed, and not always explained.
corruption_paragraphs: Two false readings compete whenever calamity strikes. The secular one calls it random, which offers no comfort and no warning. The superstitious one reads every disaster as a direct verdict on those it fell upon — a reading the Lord Jesus explicitly refused concerning the tower of Siloam, while turning it into a summons to all: except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Scripture keeps calamity meaningful without making it a scoreboard.

For the believer, Deuteronomy 32:35 and Psalm 18:18 sit together and settle the matter. The day of calamity is at hand for the wicked by appointment, not by chance; and in the day of the saint's own calamity the LORD was his stay. Neither verse promises exemption. And Proverbs 27:10 keeps the doctrine from floating free of ordinary life: the practical answer to calamity is often a neighbour close enough to reach you, which makes the cultivation of nearby friendship a matter of prudence and not merely of pleasure.
roots_summary: Hebrew eyd (H343), calamity, the day of disaster; hovah (H1943), ruin; ra'ah (H7451), evil, adversity — the general word for calamity sent or permitted.
roots_lines: Hebrew eyd (H343) — calamity, distress, the appointed day of disaster (Deu 32:35; Pro 1:26).
Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — evil, distress, adversity; the word behind Amos' question, shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it? (Amo 3:6).
Hebrew hovah (H1943) — ruin, mischief, calamity; the prophets' word for the crash that comes on a proud city.
usage: “Their foot shall slide in due time” — the wicked stand only until an appointed hour.
“They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the LORD was my stay” — the believer's testimony.
“Better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off” — calamity makes nearness precious.

pos: n. (one held in confinement; rendering Hebrew asir, Greek desmios)
etymology: From Old French prisonier, from Latin prehendere, to seize. Scripture's interest is less in the walls than in who holds the key.
biblical_def: Prisoner is a word Scripture treats with unusual tenderness. The LORD “heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners” (Psa 69:33) — and the possessive is remarkable: his prisoners, men in chains who are still His. The Psalter asks that the sighing of the prisoner come before God (Psa 79:11), declares that He hears “the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death” (Psa 102:20), and states it as a settled divine practice: “The LORD looseth the prisoners” (Psa 146:7). Job notes the grim mercy of the grave, where “the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor” (Job 3:18). Joseph is the great Old Testament instance, made keeper of the prisoners in the very house where he was one (Gen 39:22). Then Paul transfigures the word entirely, refusing to call himself Rome's prisoner at all: “I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Eph 3:1). The chain was real; the ownership was not Caesar's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prisoner as one who is confined in a prison by legal arrest or warrant, and also as a captive taken by an enemy in war — and figuratively, one held in restraint of any kind.
webster_full: PRIS´ONER, n. One who is confined in a prison by legal arrest or warrant; as a prisoner in the county jail.
2. A person under arrest or in custody of the sheriff, whether in prison or not.
3. A captive; one taken by an enemy in war.
4. One whose liberty is restrained, as a bird in a cage.
scriptures: For the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners.
Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The LORD looseth the prisoners:
Eph 3:1
For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,
Job 3:18
There the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor.
corruption_summary: Prisoners written off as a class beneath notice, or romanticized as innocents by definition — both readings evade the plain fact that Scripture calls them His and commands the church to visit them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure here is practical rather than doctrinal, and it runs in two directions. A comfortable church forgets prisoners entirely, though the Lord Jesus lists visiting them among the deeds He will name at the judgment (Mat 25:36). A sentimental one treats guilt as a social construct and loses the justice that makes mercy meaningful. Scripture holds both: the guilty are genuinely guilty, and God still hears their groaning.

The principle to recover is Psalm 69:33 — his prisoners. God does not disown men in chains, and neither may His church. Joseph's prison became the corridor to Pharaoh's throne; Paul's chain produced the prison epistles, which have done more for the church than his liberty ever did. And Paul's own refusal to name Rome as his jailer is the believer's pattern under every confinement: the circumstances belonged to Caesar, and he belonged to Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew asir (H615), a bound one, from asar, to bind; Greek desmios (G1198), one in bonds — Paul's self-designation, always with Christ named as the one who holds the chain.
roots_lines: Hebrew asir (H615) — prisoner, bondman, literally one bound; the LORD looseth them (Psa 146:7).
Greek desmios (G1198) — a prisoner, one in bonds; Paul calls himself the prisoner of Jesus Christ (Eph 3:1) and of the Lord (Eph 4:1).
Greek desmoterion (G1201) — the prison itself; where Paul and Silas sang at midnight (Act 16:26).
usage: “The LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners” — He does not disown men in chains.
“The LORD looseth the prisoners” — stated as settled divine practice.
“I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ” — the chain was Rome's; the ownership was not.
